analysis.one_liner: Restores patients' right to sue medical device makers in state court over defective devices.
analysis.headline: A bill restoring patients' right to sue over defective medical devices was referred to a House committee and never advanced.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, courts have held that FDA approval of a medical device largely shields the manufacturer from patient lawsuits under state law. This bill would change that: it amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to say that federal device rules do not limit a person's right to sue for damages under state law, and it would apply retroactively to lawsuits already in progress. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients injured or killed by defective medical devices, and their families, would regain the ability to seek compensation in state court. Today, courts have often ruled that federal approval of a device blocks those lawsuits; this bill would remove that legal shield and apply to cases already filed.

how_it_helps.text: It amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act so that federal device rules no longer shield a device maker from liability for damages under state law.
It applies to civil actions pending or filed after enactment, reviving claims for people already injured and already in court.

analysis.who_pays: Medical device manufacturers, which would face damage lawsuits in state courts for devices they sell, including suits over devices already approved by the FDA. Any litigation costs would partly flow into device prices.

drawbacks.text: Device manufacturers argued that restoring parallel state-law damage claims would expose them to costly litigation and inconsistent state jury verdicts, potentially raising device prices and dampening innovation.
The bill applies retroactively and to lawsuits already pending, which changes the legal rules for cases that had already been filed, a feature critics of retroactive liability often object to.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would have been real: injured patients and their families could once again seek compensation when a defective device harms them, restoring a remedy the Supreme Court's reading of current law forecloses in many cases [S2][S3]. The cost, in makers' telling, is greater liability exposure that could discourage innovation and raise device prices; honest supporters of liability rules generally accept some price and uncertainty cost as the price of accountability. The main design criticism of the bill itself is the retroactive application to pending lawsuits, which changes the rules mid-case for companies and courts [S2]. On balance, for ordinary patients the benefits outweighed those costs, which is precisely why the bill's death without a hearing or vote mattered.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 26, 2017 by Rep. Fitzpatrick, joined by Reps. Slaughter and DeLauro.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and a week later to that committee's Health Subcommittee.
No further action was taken: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — the bill died in subcommittee when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medical device makers are better off, because the legal shield protecting them from patient lawsuits survives.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore state-law liability for defective medical devices.

for.name: Reps. Louise Slaughter and Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee / Subcommittee on Health
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, allowing the bill to expire without action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican lead sponsor and four Democratic cosponsors, giving it bipartisan origins, but with so few cosponsors and no recorded votes the partisan shape of the broader House is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would strip away the legal preemption that currently protects device makers from most state-law damage suits over FDA-approved devices, exposing them to jury verdicts for injured patients. Because the bill died, that shield remains in place.

industries.industry: Product-liability defense bar and device-industry insurers
industries.note: The industry's legal-defense infrastructure loses the business that state-court damage suits would generate; with the bill dead, this system remains intact.
